spans.assertion: the analysis used data from the 2012-2013 season across four leagues (England, France, Germany, Spain), covering 146,028 player-referee dyads
used the pre-specified binary skin-tone classification (dark >0.5, light ≤0.5) for the primary analysis
the adjusted risk difference was 0.098 percentage points (95% CI -0.076 to 0.273, p=0.269), not statistically significant at α=0.05
the primary analysis's hypothesis is not supported because the CI includes zero and p exceeds the conventional threshold, so the observed difference could plausibly be due to chance
sensitivity analyses using alternative skin tone definitions (continuous, extremes) yielded statistically significant results (p=0.009 and p=0.021)
suggests the null primary finding may reflect loss of statistical power from dichotomization rather than a true absence of effect
defined the primary estimand as the adjusted risk difference comparing dark-skinned (>0.5) to light-skinned (≤0.5) players, adjusted for confounders
adjusted risk difference = 0.0983 percentage points
95% CI for adjusted risk difference = [-0.0761, 0.2726] percentage points
z-statistic = 1.1045
two-sided p-value at α=0.05 = 0.2694

after adjustment, dark-skinned players have an estimated 0.10 percentage-point higher probability of a red card than light-skinned players, a non-significant difference with 95% CI spanning -0.08 to +0.27 pp
defined the secondary estimand as the adjusted odds ratio for red card, dark vs light skin tone, adjusted for confounders
adjusted odds ratio = 1.0843
95% CI for adjusted odds ratio = [0.9389, 1.2521]
two-sided p-value = 0.2705
odds of a red card are 8.4% higher for dark-skinned players after adjustment, consistent with the risk-difference result, and not statistically significant since the CI includes 1.0
defined the unit of analysis as the player-referee dyad, a unique pairing across all games they encountered each other
total dyads analyzed N = 123,868
19,726 dyads (15.93%) were dark-skinned-player dyads
104,142 dyads (84.07%) were light-skinned-player dyads
1,562 dyads (1.26%) had a red-card event
measured skin tone as the average of two independent raters' assessments on a 0-1 scale, normalized from an original 5-point scale
classified players as light skin if average rating ≤0.5 and dark skin if >0.5
raters were blind to the research question and rated players from profile photos
defined the outcome as a binary indicator of whether any red card was received in the dyad across all encounters
adjusted the model for a specified set of confounders
included number of games between the player-referee pair as a continuous covariate, as a proxy for exposure time
included player position as a categorical covariate with 12 specific positions plus an Unknown category
included league country (England, France, Germany, Spain) as a categorical covariate
included player height (cm) as a continuous covariate
included player weight (kg) as a continuous covariate
included yellow cards as a continuous covariate, as a proxy for player aggression/foul tendency
included goals scored as a continuous covariate, as a proxy for offensive play style
used logistic regression estimated via maximum likelihood as the primary model
computed average marginal effects via counterfactual exposure assignment (all dark-skinned vs all light-skinned) and averaged the difference
used cluster-robust (Huber-White sandwich) standard errors clustered by referee
sample contained 2,968 unique referees

spans.note: explains rationale for clustering by referee

spans.assertion: used two-sided Wald tests at α=0.05 for inference
excluded 21,407 dyads (14.66% of the original dataset) for missing skin-tone ratings
photos were available for only 1,586 of 2,053 players
excluded a further 753 dyads (0.60% of those with skin-tone ratings) for missing height or weight
total of 22,160 dyads (15.18% of original 146,028) were excluded
averaged the two rater skin-tone assessments and dichotomized at the 0.5 threshold
converted red-card count to a binary outcome (any vs none)
coded missing position values as an 'Unknown' category
applied no other transformations; all continuous variables were entered linearly
unadjusted red-card rate for light-skinned players = 1.2493% (1,301/104,142)
unadjusted red-card rate for dark-skinned players = 1.3231% (261/19,726)
unadjusted risk difference = 0.0739 percentage points
unadjusted chi-square test: χ²=0.75, p=0.385
the unadjusted difference is smaller than the adjusted difference, suggesting negative confounding (dark-skinned players have somewhat more favorable distributions of some risk factors)
mean games played were 3.02 for light-skinned and 2.89 for dark-skinned players, i.e. dark-skinned players played slightly fewer games
mean yellow cards were 0.41 for light-skinned and 0.36 for dark-skinned players, i.e. dark-skinned players had slightly fewer yellow cards

position distribution differs substantially by skin tone: dark-skinned players are more often Center Forwards (20.5% vs 12.1%), and less often Goalkeepers (2.0% vs 10.2%) or Attacking Midfielders (3.4% vs 9.7%)
league distribution differs substantially by skin tone: dark-skinned players are more common in England and France, and less common in Germany and Spain, with specific percentages given
these covariate imbalances justify the need for covariate adjustment
